newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: PBOC's Guo You details China/HK money relationship.
newsitem.headline: PBOC's Guo You details China/HK money relationship.

text.p: There are seven major princples governing the monetary relationship between mainland China and Hong Kong given that there is already the legal foundation for defining the "one country, two currencies" relationship, a Chinese bank official said.

Guo You, Deputy Director of the Foreign Financial Institutions Department of the People's Bank of China told a conference in Singapore, "This relationship can be best summarized as one country, two currencies, two monetary systems and two monetary authorities under two different social and economic systems within a sovereign state."

He said while the Hong Kong dollar and the yuan will remain independent of each other, both will circulate as legal tender in Hong Kong and the mainland respectively while the dollar will be treated as foreign currency on the mainland, but the linked exchange rate system will continue.

Secondly, the People's Bank of China (PBOC) and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will function independently and the PBOC will not take the place of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority and will not even set up an office there.

Third, the Hong Kong government will continue to supervise the financial sector including institutions from the mainland and if financial institutions from the mainland set up offices in Hong Kong, or vice-verca, they will be treated as foreign financal institutions.
Fourth, the PBOC will support the currency stability of Hong Kong and under no circumstances will China draw on, or resort to, Hong Kong's exchange fund or other assets.
Fifth, claims and liabilities between the mainland and Hong Kong will be arranged in accordance with international financial practices and Chinese entities will have no special privileges.
Sixth, mainland financial institutions in Hong Kong will be regulated by Hong Kong and will not be treated more favorable than other financial institutions.

Lastly, Shanghai is reviving itself as China's financal centre but in the short-term, at least until yuan become fully covertible, it will not be possible for Shanghai to become an international financial centre.
But given the size of China's economy there is room for more than one financal centre and Hong Kong and Shanghai will become two complementary financial centres, Guo said.
"We project an average of around 8.0 percent growth (in China) and inflation below 5-6 percent in the next five years or even longer," Dr Guo said.
"To realise that target there is plenty of work to be done on monetary policy, however, with Hong Kong coming back, with a combined effort, we feel more confident to meet the challenge."
